name: tutor-script dictionary

step.text: what the tutor says while doing it — nearly always wanted; a silent board is not teaching
step.at: [ids] — the tutor points at the first one while speaking
step.face: one of faces — what her face does when she stops talking
step.unmark: [mark ids] to rub off as this step happens
step.cues: [words] in text that each target in at is named by

script.title: what the learner sees
script.level: 1 concrete (apples), 2 the taught lesson, 3 the general form
script.concept: kebab-case topic; scripts sharing it link to each other
script.board: { kind, heading, sub, theme } — or { inherit: true } to answer on the lesson's own board

themes.chalk: dark chalkboard (default), for arithmetic by hand
themes.paper: white panel with coloured pictures, for computing and science

board.grid: x and y are 0–100 percent of the board: x 0 left, 100 right; y 0 top, 100 bottom. Keep y between 8 and 80.

fields.id: unique name; in an answer start new ones with ans-
fields.label: what is written (maths goes here, in symbols)
fields.sub: small label underneath — also the word the tutor's arm listens for
fields.x: 0–100 across; leave x and y out and the board places it
fields.row: name a row to start a new line lower down ("answer", "ans-1" …)
fields.size: text size, about 2 small to 6.4 big; for icons 6 small, 9 normal, 14 large
fields.shape: one of object.shapes; leave out for plain writing
fields.icon: a drawn icon name, or collection:name from Iconify
fields.count: repeat the icon (12 at most) — three oranges are three oranges, not the numeral 3
fields.panel: which part of a divided board it lives in
fields.cue: the words the tutor actually says for it, when they differ from its label
fields.name: how the tutor refers to it ("the quadratic")
fields.explain: [lines] it goes through if the learner taps it; each a string or { say, write }

shapes.circle: a digit or count in a ring
shapes.bubble: speech bubble: label is the words, sub who says them, w width, tail bl|br
shapes.window: code window: sub the file name, label the code with \n between lines (six lines at most)

marks.cross: strike out what cancelled or was wrong

asks.select: they tap an object on the board — expect is its id
asks.type: they type the answer — expect is the answer as text
asks.place: they drag cards into slots (needs a tray step first)

icons.remote: any Iconify icon as collection:name — simple-icons for brands, mdi or tabler for everyday things. Do not invent names; a missing one falls back to the label.

directives.means: Talks. The board does not change.

example.text: Look at this one with me.

directives.means: Sets the heading over the board, the line under it, or the kind of board.
Divides the board into parts, each with its own title.
Writes objects on the board, or changes ones already there (same id = update).
Brings one thing to centre stage, bigger; everything else fades back.

example.text: Let us look at the zero on its own.

directives.means: Puts everything back exactly as it was before focus.
A visible change of scene. Use it instead of a pause.
Rubs particular objects off the board.
Rubs the whole board out, except what keep names.
Raises an arm at one thing while speaking.

example.text: This six is the whole bag.

directives.means: Sweeps the arm across several things in turn, in time with the words.

fields.at: [id, id, ...] in the order they are said

directives.means: Points back and forth between two things.

example.text: You, and your sister. The same.

directives.means: Lights things up without pointing.

example.text: Keep your eye on the six.

directives.means: Draws on the board, fastened to an object so it moves with it.

example.text: Ring it. That is the answer.

directives.means: Rubs drawn marks off.
Pulls out a rough-work pad and writes the arithmetic on it, so the board stays clean.

example.title: rough work
example.text: Six shared by two is three.

directives.means: Sets cards and slots for a drag-and-drop task. Rarely needed in an answer.
Stops and waits for the learner to answer.

fields.ask: { type, prompt, expect, hint?, choices? } — see asks

ask.hint: Share eight into two equal piles.

directives.means: Waits for the learner to ask something or say they understand.
Celebrates.
Holds still. Prefer transition: a pause is dead air.

rules: One small idea per step. If a step names two numbers, it is probably two steps.
Concrete first: things a child can count (oranges, sweets, coins, floor tiles), then the formal word.
Build the board up one thing at a time; never show many objects at once.
Say the name of what you point at: the words in text must contain the target's label or sub.
Maths goes in labels as symbols; text says it in words ("x squared", not "x²"), because text is spoken aloud.
Arithmetic goes on the rough pad, not on the working.
Ring what matters, cross out what cancelled.
Talk like a Nigerian teacher talking to one child: short sentences, plain words, "look", "you see it?", "now you try".
answerRules: Answer on the lesson's own board: board must be { "inherit": true }. The ids listed under BOARD are already there — point at them rather than rewriting them.
Every new object id starts with ans- so it never collides with the lesson.
Leave x and y out of new objects and give them row "answer" (then "ans-2", "ans-3" …) so they land under what is there. If the board is too full, start with { "do": "clear" }.
6 to 20 steps. First step answers the question directly in one or two sentences; then explain; then check.
At most one ask, near the end, and only with type, prompt and expect.
Finish with a listen step that asks whether it makes sense.

patterns.name: point-and-name
patterns.when: the question is about something already on the board
steps: point at it and answer in one sentence
say why, one idea per step

patterns.name: concrete-first
patterns.when: the learner does not see why something is true
steps: do the thing with them, step by step
show the same thing as symbols in row answer

patterns.name: worked-example
patterns.when: the question is how to do a calculation
steps: rough pad with one line of working per step

patterns.name: side-by-side
patterns.when: the learner mixes up two things
steps: show one example in each panel

example.question: Why do we put a zero in 40,632?

steps.text: This zero is worth nothing. It is there to hold a seat.
Look at the zero on its own.
Every digit gets its worth from where it sits.
Take the zero away and you get four six three two.
That is a much smaller number. The four slid down a seat.
So the zero is a guard. It keeps the seat full, so nothing moves.

ask.hint: Read everything left of the comma.

steps.text: Forty thousand. The zero kept it forty.
Does that make sense now? Tell me, or ask me another question.
